In a Mist is dated September 8 by the sessionography and September 9 by the booklet and Wikipedia, so only the month is kept.

You Sweet Thing, Blue Drag, I Love You Because I Love You, Sensational Mood, My One Ambition, plus piano solos Love Me Tonight and Down Among the Sheltering Palms), and Feb 13, 1933 (Rosetta, Why Must We Part?, Maybe I'm to Blame, Cavernism).

Corrections to the MusicBrainz draft: the 1929 drummer is Benny Washington (drums, vibraphone), not Wallace Bishop, who joined by 1932; Hayes Alvis (tuba) is on all the 1929 band sides; Billy and William Franklin are one trombonist; Love Me Tonight and Down Among the Sheltering Palms are Hines solos, not band sides; Glad Rag Doll is a solo; Charlie Allen and George Dixon (trumpets), Quinn Wilson (bass) and Darnell Howard (reeds) are on all the 1932-33 sides; Jimmy Mundy and Valaida Snow only on Feb 13, 1933.

Dates: Mosaic dates the first OKeh solos Dec 11, 1928 from the OKeh file cards; earlier discographies say Dec 9 (MusicBrainz had Dec 8 and 9). Mosaic notes the two Brunswick test recordings of July 14, 1932 (a take of I Love You Because I Love You and My One Ambition) may come from another day.

Vocals: Billy Franklin (Sweet Ella May; the alternate of Good Little, Bad Little You), Hayes Alvis (the issued Good Little, Bad Little You), Hines (Everybody Loves My Baby, Have You Ever Felt That Way, Sister Kate), Walter Fuller (I Love You Because I Love You, My One Ambition, the vocal takes of Rosetta), Valaida Snow (Maybe I'm to Blame).

Left out: an unidentified guitarist Mosaic adds to the Feb 15, 1929 session (Beau-Koo Jack, Sister Kate). Jack Kapp or Victor Young supervised the Brunswick dates, Mosaic says, without knowing which, so neither is credited.

Several titles appear in more than one take (Everybody Loves My Baby, Sister Kate, I Love You Because I Love You, Rosetta and others); credits are matched by title, which is right here since every take of a title has the same band. Apple's take labels don't always match Mosaic's (Mosaic's issued Good Little, Bad Little You is take 3, the alternate take 2).

draftNotes: Nine sessions, all New York: two Brunswick dates in 1933 (a quintet with Jimmy Dorsey; the 'chamber jazz' quartet with Benny Goodman on bass clarinet), the Columbia Swing Septet of Sept 26 and Oct 4, 1934 (Shaw, Barnet, Jenney, Teddy Wilson), the Swing Octet of Jan 25, 1935 (Berigan, Chu Berry, Krupa), and the 1936 Decca band with Eddie Sauter's arrangements (Jan 6, Jan 8, Feb 26 and the Swing Sextette of Mar 16).

The draft had the right regulars but missed the 1933 players (Jimmy Dorsey, Fulton McGrath, Dick McDonough, Benny Goodman), the 1934 septet (Shaw, Barnet, Bobby Johnson, Hank Wayland, Billy Gussak), the 1935 octet (Berigan, Mince, Chu Berry, Van Eps, Krupa), Howard Smith, and gave Norvo piano.

Hep's Discogs credits omit Artie Bernstein on the two 1933 quartet sides and Dick McDonough on the first session; Classics 1085, Wikipedia and Lord-derived listings have both, and the Syncopated Times review calls the sessions a quintet and a quartet, so both are kept. The first session is dated April 18 by Hep and April 8 by DAHR (matrix B13206) and Lord; April 8 kept.

Hep credits Norvo on piano on the Feb 26, 1936 sides; DAHR's Ruppli notes have him on xylophone with no pianist, so piano is dropped. Hep also lists Eddie Sauter on the Mar 16, 1936 sextet sides; DAHR's note for Oh, Lady Be Good doesn't, so he is left off them.

Vocals: Mae Questel on The Music Goes 'Round and Around and The Broken Record (Classics and Hep; DAHR files matrix 60316 under Questel's name). Stew Pletcher sings on You Started Me Dreaming and What's the Name of That Song (DAHR); Classics credits him on all six Feb 26 sides, Hep on the January sides, so only the two DAHR confirms are kept. Polly Wolly Doodle and The Wedding of Jack and Jill have an unnamed vocal trio, not listed.
Columbia dates (Sept 26 and Oct 4, 1934) and the Nov 21, 1933 date come from Hep's notes only.

draftNotes: Eleven sessions: Teddy Hill's orchestra (May 17, 1937), Lionel Hampton's all-stars on Hot Mallets (Sept 11, 1939), the 52nd Street sextet with Don Byas and Milt Jackson (Feb 22, 1946), the big band (Aug 22 and Dec 22 and 30, 1947; Dec 29, 1948; April 14, May 6 and July 6, 1949) and the Metronome All-Stars (Jan 3, 1949). Players put on their sessions' tracks from jazzdisco; Wikipedia's per-track list agrees.

Don Byas sits out both Anthropology takes; on the Victory Ball shorter take the Metronome band is reduced (no Miles Davis, Fats Navarro, J.J. Johnson or Ernie Caceres), per jazzdisco. Dizzy sings on Oop-Pop-A-Da, Cool Breeze, Ool-Ya-Koo, both I'm Be Boppin' Too takes, Jump Did-Le Ba and Hey Pete; Chano Pozo chants on Cubana Bop; Joe Harris plays drums in 1947 and conga in December 1948.
I'm Be Boppin' Too take 2 has the 1948 matrix (D8VB4151-2) but jazzdisco and Wikipedia list it with the May 6, 1949 session; it's credited to the May 1949 band.

The draft's producers (Orrin Keepnews, Brian Bacchus) and designer made the 1995 reissue, so they were dropped. Arrangers: Gil Fuller, Pete Rugolo (Overtime) and Lennie Tristano (Victory Ball) are from the draft's MusicBrainz credits; George Russell (Cubana Be / Cubana Bop) was added. Billy Bauer's arranger credit in the draft wasn't confirmed and was dropped.
Howard Johnson (alto) is the same player in 1937 and 1947 (Wikipedia links both to Howard E. Johnson).

draftNotes: Rebuilt by hand: the MusicBrainz draft credited only Shaw (on 8 tracks). Every track was matched to its master in the Scheer-Hennings & Spragg sessionographies, whose issue lists name this CD (Bluebird 82876 69239-2) for 35 of the 38 tracks; personnel are theirs, from the RCA session sheets, and agree with the label's per-track credits where Qobuz shows them.

Bands: the 1938-39 'Great Band' (Jul 24, Sep 27, Nov 17, Dec 19 1938; Jan 31, Mar 12-13, Jun 12 in Hollywood, Aug 27, Oct 26 1939), with its changes followed session by session (Koenig for Robinson and Russ Brown for Ted Vesely in Sep 1938; Privin, Les Jenkins, Kitsis, Wettling and Auld by Dec 19; Buddy Rich from Jan 1939; Harry Geller for John Best from Aug 1939); the Hollywood studio orchestras of Mar 3-4 1940 (Frenesi) and May 13-14 1940 (April in Paris); the Gramercy Five of Sep 3 and Dec 5 1940 (Butterfield, Guarnieri on harpsichord, Hendrickson, DeNaut, Fatool); the strings band of Sep 1940-Jan 1941 (Temptation, Star Dust, Concerto for Clarinet, Dancing in the Dark); the Lena Horne date of Jun 26 1941 (Red Allen, Higginbotham, Benny Carter); the fall 1941 band with Hot Lips Page (Blues in the Night, Take Your Shoes Off Baby in Chicago, St. James Infirmary); and the 1945 band (Tabu) and Gramercy Five (Scuttlebutt) with Roy Eldridge, Dodo Marmarosa and Barney Kessel.

String sections are left out to keep the list readable: about 13 players on Frenesi, 10 on April in Paris, 9 on the Sep 1940-Jan 1941 sides, 13 on Don't Take Your Love from Me and 15 on the fall 1941 sides (the sessionographies name them; for Sep 2-3 1941 they're unidentified).

Georgia on My Mind (Mar 20, 1941, New York): the sessionography gives only probable personnel ('probably' Butterfield, Jenney, Conniff, Robinson; Jerry Jerome; Guarnieri and Fatool; no guitar), while MusicBrainz lists a full band (Privin, Castle, Mondello, Sam Herman on guitar, McKinney). Only Shaw, Johnny Guarnieri and Nick Fatool, whom the sessionography states firmly, are credited.

Three tracks fall outside the sessionographies: Streamline (Art Shaw and His Strings, Brunswick; the players are the edition's own credits; its date isn't established, so the session is entered as 1936, the year the MusicBrainz annotation's range starts and the Classics chronology places it); Shoot the Likker to Me, John Boy (Art Shaw and His New Music, Vocalion 4198, Sep 17, 1937 per FAU's Recorded Sound Archives; the edition gives no personnel and none per session was found, so only Shaw is credited); These Foolish Things (Shaw recorded it for Victor on Jun 8, 1945 and for Decca on Jul 2, 1953; the sessionography doesn't list this CD for the Victor master and reviews say the set runs to 1953, so which one this is isn't settled and only Shaw is credited, with no session entered).

Disagreements: the 1945 tenor on Tabu is Ralph Rosenlund per the RCA session sheets (and the label credits), but historians quoted by Spragg say Herbie Steward stayed with the band; Augostino Ischia is the trombonist's name on the session sheets (other sources name a Gus Dixon/Dickson in the section). Frenesi's Jack Stacy is tenor in the sessionography, alto in the label credits. The sessionography prints the Concerto for Clarinet date as Dec 17, 1941, a typo for 1940 (it sits between the Dec 5, 1940 and Jan 23, 1941 sessions).

Billie Holiday sings Any Old Time; Helen Forrest Deep Purple, All the Things You Are, Deep in a Dream and A Room With a View; Tony Pastor Indian Love Call and You're a Lucky Guy; Lena Horne Don't Take Your Love from Me; Hot Lips Page Blues in the Night, Take Your Shoes Off Baby and St. James Infirmary. Arrangers credited are those the sessionographies name on these masters.

draftNotes: Rebuilt session by session (45 sessions, 1926-1943). Disc 1 is Waller's own songs, disc 2 instrumentals (one pipe-organ solo, ten piano solos, small groups and big band), disc 3 Tin Pan Alley songs. Waller is on every track: piano and vocals, pipe organ on St. Louis Blues (1926 solo) and the Louisiana Sugar Babes sides ('Sippi, Thou Swell, 1928, with Jabbo Smith, Garvin Bushell and James P. Johnson), Hammond organ on Mamacita, The Jitterbug Waltz and (per MusicBrainz) Let's Get Away from It All, celesta on Rosetta and Sugar Rose.

St. Louis Blues here is the November 1926 pipe-organ solo (Qobuz credits pipe organ only; Qobuz's description counts 'one organ and ten piano solos' on disc 2), not the 1929 piano duet with Bennie Paine, which is not on this set.

Fixed from the draft: Al Casey was credited on trumpet (a MusicBrainz error, guitar only); the per-track credits are now by session. Disc 3 opens with Jack Teagarden's Columbia orchestra of October 1931 (You Rascal You, Waller piano and vocal with Teagarden); disc 2 ends with the March 1937 'Jam Session at Victor' Honeysuckle Rose (Berigan, Tommy Dorsey, McDonough, Wettling).

Big-band sessions list only players the sources agree on. Functionizin' (Dec 4, 1935): the 1982 Bluebird LP and Classics name Sidney De Paris and Clarence Smith (trumpets) and Don Redman (alto), Qobuz has Ed Anderson and C.E. Smith ('probably'), Fred Robinson, George James and Fred Skerritt; only Autrey, Morton, Powell, Matthews, Sedric, Carroll, Duncan (second piano), James Smith, Turner and Porter are kept (Qobuz omits Morton and Carroll). Bluebird and Classics also credit Waller on vibraphone there; left out. Ain't Nothin' to It: Qobuz adds a third trumpet, Bob Williams. March 16, 1942 (You Must Be Losing Your Mind, The Jitterbug Waltz): MusicBrainz adds Herman Autrey, Nathaniel Williams, Jackie Fields and Slick Jones and Qobuz adds Courtney Williams; left out. DAHR files Jitterbug Waltz as 'Fats Waller and his Rhythm', other catalogs as 'his Rhythm and his Orchestra'. April 12, 1938: RCA's French Indispensable 5/6 names the tenor 'Samuel Simons' where Qobuz and MusicBrainz have Lonnie Simmons.

Drummers: I'm Crazy 'Bout My Baby (Aug 1, 1936) has Slick Jones per MusicBrainz and RCA's Indispensable credits, Yank Porter per Qobuz. Lounging at the Waldorf (June 8, 1936) has Yank Porter per Qobuz and MusicBrainz; the June 5 and April 8 sessions have Arnold Boling. Dinah (June 24, 1935): Qobuz shows Mezz Mezzrow and Billy Taylor, apparently copied from the 1934 session; MusicBrainz's Rudy Powell, James Smith, Charles Turner and Arnold Boling kept.

Disc 3 tracks 7-22 rest on MusicBrainz alone (Qobuz's page stops at track 6), with the session lineups consistent with the neighbouring sessions. She's Tall, She's Tan, She's Terrific lacks Herman Autrey in MusicBrainz; he is kept because he is on the other title of that session (Sept 7, 1937). Blue, Turnin' Grey Over You had no MusicBrainz credits; it is the June 11, 1937 Rhythm side (Classics 838, Qobuz).

Ain't Misbehavin' (disc 1 track 22) is the 1943 Stormy Weather film recording with Benny Carter's group (Qobuz and MusicBrainz agree on the players); MusicBrainz dates it January 23, 1943, kept as just the year. Gene Porter's instrument isn't given by Qobuz; clarinet assumed from MusicBrainz's 'reeds'.

Two titles appear twice and credits are matched by title: Honeysuckle Rose (1934 Rhythm, disc 1; 1937 jam session, disc 2) and Ain't Misbehavin' (1943 band, disc 1; 1929 solo, disc 2), so each version's players show on both.

Places: most Victor/Bluebird sessions were in New York (Victor Studio 2 for the 1941-42 dates); the place of the July 1941 big-band date isn't documented in the sources checked. No crew: the set was compiled by Orrin Keepnews and the original sessions' supervisors (e.g. Leonard Joy) aren't documented per session in the sources checked.

zodiac-suite.source: Smithsonian Folkways SF CD 40810 booklet (credits; Dan Morgenstern's track notes), read from folkways-media.si.edu; Discogs releases 2401280, 525085 and 8916559
draftNotes: The MusicBrainz draft had matched a 2023 French big-band recording of the suite; rebuilt for the Apple edition, which is Smithsonian Folkways' 1995 CD of the 1945 Asch trio session: the twelve signs, six of them (Aries, Gemini, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Aquarius) in previously unissued takes, then the issued takes of Aries, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio and Aquarius (tracks 13-17).

Who plays where, from Morgenstern's notes in the booklet: Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius and Pisces are piano solos; the alternate Aries and the alternate Virgo are duets with Al Lucas; the alternate Cancer is with bass only, and Parker's brushes join after Lucas's solo on the issued Cancer; Taurus ('dig the rhythm section'), Leo (opens with a drum roll) and Scorpio are trios. Capricorn is counted as the fifth solo by elimination (Wikipedia, after Kernodle: six trio pieces, five solos, one duet); the notes don't say.

Jack Parker is credited only on Taurus, Leo and Scorpio. He is also on the issued Cancer (track 14), but credits are matched by title and the alternate Cancer (track 4) has no drums, so he is left off it; whether he plays on Gemini and the issued Aries and Virgo isn't stated.
Date: the booklet says 'Recorded at Asch Records Studio, New York, Spring, 1945'; Discogs' notes for the CD and the 1946 Asch 78 albums say June 1945. Only the year is kept.

draftNotes: No MusicBrainz draft; written from the discographies. Apple's order is chronological: Gennett, April 5-6 (1-9); OKeh, June 22-23 (10-16); Gennett, October 5 (17-20, with Stump Evans and Charlie Jackson added and Johnny St. Cyr on banjo); Columbia, October 15-16 (21-24); OKeh, October (25-32); Paramount (33-35); then Oliver with Butterbeans and Susie and Clarence Williams (Kiss Me Sweet, Construction Gang, OKeh, New York, September 12, 1924) and his two duets with Jelly Roll Morton (King Porter Stomp, Tom Cat Blues, Autograph, Chicago, December 1924). The '[Live]' tags on Snake Rag and Mabel's Dream are Apple metadata; every side is a studio recording.

Banjo, April 1923: Bill Johnson (most accounts, and the Syncopated Times on the first line-up) against Bud Scott (Minn); Off the Record lists both. Bud Scott replaced Johnson by the June OKeh sides. Bill Johnson's and Bud Scott's 'Oh, play that thing!' breaks on the two Dipper Mouth Blues aren't listed as vocals.

Columbia, October 1923: Ed Atkins replaces Dutrey and Jimmie Noone plays clarinet on Chattanooga Stomp (15th). On the 16th (London Cafe Blues, Camp Meeting Blues, New Orleans Stomp) the clarinetist is disputed: Lord, Willems and de Davrichewy say Noone, Allen/Rust/Wright and the Off the Record booklet say Buster Bailey. Neither is listed for those three; Johnny Dodds disclaimed them.

Dates in dispute: the second OKeh pair is October 25-26 for Westerberg and Off the Record, early to mid October for Willems and de Davrichewy, so only the month is given; the Paramount session is December 24 for Westerberg and early September for de Davrichewy and Willems, so only the year. Minn has no banjo on the Paramount sides; MusicBrainz's Bill Johnson there is left out.

Same titles, different sessions: Snake Rag and Dipper Mouth Blues (Gennett and OKeh), Riverside Blues and Mabel's Dream (OKeh and Paramount). Credits are matched by title, so each version shows the players of both (the banjoist is the only difference).

Construction Gang: DAHR credits Oliver's cornet on both Butterbeans and Susie sides; a 45worlds label transcription describes it as with piano only. Kept on both. Louis Armstrong's slide whistle is on Sobbin' Blues (Minn).

draftNotes: Written from scratch (no MusicBrainz draft). Nine all-star Victor sessions, matched to the Apple tracklist in order: Feb 8, 1937 (Goodman's band: Elman, Schertzer, Koenig, Musso, Rollini, Stacy, Reuss, Harry Goodman, Krupa); Apr 14, 1937 and Jan 18, 1938 (Ellingtonians Cootie Williams, Lawrence Brown / Edgar Sampson, Johnny Hodges, Sonny Greer); Apr 26, 1937 (Buster Bailey, Hodges, Stacy, Reuss, Kirby, Cole); Aug 16 and Sep 5, 1937 in Hollywood; Jul 21, 1938 (Harry James, Benny Carter, Herschel Evans, Billy Kyle, Kirby, Jo Jones); Oct 11, 1938 (Earl Hines's band: Walter Fuller, Omer Simeon, Budd Johnson, Alvin Burroughs); Apr 3, 1939 (Chu Berry, Jerry Jerome, Clyde Hart, Milt Hinton, Cozy Cole).

Per-track changes from Mosaic's notes: Hampton plays drums in place of Krupa on Hampton Stomp (issued as "Stomp") and in place of Cole on I Know That You Know and Drum Stomp; Hodges sits out China Stomp (Hampton and Stacy both at the piano); Hampton adds piano on Piano Stomp and Rock Hill Special. Hampton's drums and piano are listed among his instruments, since instruments aren't per track.

Alternate takes on the Apple edition: My Last Affair takes 1 and 2, The Object of My Affection takes 1 and 2 (track 23), The Sun Will Shine Tonight take 1 (previously unissued), and the second It Don't Mean a Thing (take 2, previously unissued); each is from the same session as its issued take, so the shared titles carry the same players.
Left out: Mezz Mezzrow, whom the Bluebird booklet lists on the Apr 14, 1937 date; Mosaic says he is listed but not audible.

Sources disagree on places and one date: Mosaic's web listing puts Aug 16 and Sep 5, 1937 in New York, but the Bluebird booklet and DAHR (PBS- matrices) say Hollywood, which is kept. The Bluebird booklet dates the Ellington-men session Jan 19, 1938; DAHR and Mosaic say Jan 18, which is kept. Mosaic gives Hymie Schertzer and Russell Procope clarinet as well as alto on Apr 3, 1939; the booklet alto only.

Crew: Mosaic names Leonard Joy as supervisor (Feb 8, Apr 14 with Eli Oberstein, Apr 26 1937; Jan 18, 1938; Apr 3, 1939); the other dates name none. Arrangers documented: Edgar Sampson (Don't Be That Way, probably the whole Jan 1938 date), Benny Carter (I'm in the Mood for Swing, Any Time At All), Fred Norman (High Society). Budd Johnson is only the probable arranger of the Oct 1938 date, so not credited.

draftNotes: No draft existed; written from jazzdisco's Savoy sessions. Oct 30, 1945 quartet (Blow Mr. Dexter, Dexter's Deck, Dexter's Minor Mad, Dexter's Cuttin' Out) with Sadik Hakim, credited then as Argonne Thornton; Jan 29, 1946 quintet (Long Tall Dexter, Dexter Rides Again, I Can't Escape From You, Dexter Digs In) with Leonard Hawkins and Bud Powell's trio-mates; Dec 11, 1947 with Leo Parker and Tadd Dameron (Dexter's Riff, So Easy, Settin' the Pace); Dec 22, 1947 'Dexter Gordon and His Boys' (Dexter's Mood, Dextrose, Index, Dextivity).
Leonard Hawkins sits out I Can't Escape From You, and Fats Navarro sits out Dexter's Mood (jazzdisco).
No producer is credited: Teddy Reig ran many Savoy dates then, but no source checked names him for these; Ozzie Cadena produced only the 1958 Dexter Rides Again LP compilation.
